## Purpose of model
The purpose of this model is to understand the drivers of the expected Australian 10-year Treasury Yield.

This model is specified as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
Australian\,10\,Year\,Treasury\,Yield\ = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{US 10 Year Yield} + \epsilon_i
\end{aligned}
$$
```{r, echo=FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
## Load libraries
library(readxl)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(dplyr)
library(broom)
library(ggfortify)
library(GGally)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)
library(marginaleffects)
library(readr)
library(this.path)

## Import data
Data_FI <- read_excel("../Data/FI_AU.xlsx")

## Import test data
Data_FI_Test <- read_excel("../Data/FI_Test_AU.xlsx")

```

## Fit the model

```{r, echo=FALSE}

## Fit the model
FI.lm <- lm(GACGB10 ~ USGG10YR_Index,data = Data_FI)
summary(FI.lm)
cat("AIC: ", AIC(FI.lm), "\n")
cat("BIC: ", BIC(FI.lm), "\n")

```

## Prediction using the latest data

```{r , echo=FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

pred.new.data <- Data_FI_Test

cat("Confidence Interval:", "\n")
predict_norm <- predict(FI.lm, newdata = pred.new.data, interval = "confidence")
colnames(predict_norm) <- c("Fit", "Lower", "Upper")
print(predict_norm)

cat("\n")
cat("Using latest data: ", as.character(pred.new.data$Date), "\n")
print(as.data.frame(pred.new.data[, c(2:ncol(pred.new.data))]))


```

## Correcting for Autocorrelation and Heteroscedasticity

To correct for autocorrelation, use Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent (HAC) standard errors, which adjust statistical inference (like t-stats and p-values) without changing the OLS coefficients themselves.

The most common HAC estimator is the Newey-West estimator. It accounts for both the clustering of errors over time (autocorrelation) and unequal variance (heteroscedasticity).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
hac_FI.lm <- coeftest(FI.lm, vcov = NeweyWest(FI.lm))

print(hac_FI.lm)

HAC_preds <- predictions(FI.lm, vcov = NeweyWest, newdata = pred.new.data)
predict_HAC_preds <- HAC_preds[, c("estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
colnames(predict_HAC_preds) <- c("HAC_Estimate", "HAC_Lower", "HAC_Upper")

print(data.frame(predict_HAC_preds))

```

## Check for Autocorrelation

The Durbin-Watson test checks for first-order autocorrelation in the residuals of the model (which is especially important for time-series data).

* Null Hypothesis (H0): Residuals are uncorrelated (autocorrelation = 0).
* Alternative Hypothesis (HA): Autocorrelation exists (can be "greater", "less", or "two-sided").

Interpretation:

* P-value < 0.05: Reject the null hypothesis. There is significant evidence of autocorrelation.
* P-value > 0.05: Fail to reject the null hypothesis. The assumption of no autocorrelation holds.

In the dwtest() function from the lmtest package, you can specify the direction using the alternative argument:

* Two-sided: dwtest(model, alternative = "two.sided")
* Positive only: dwtest(model, alternative = "greater") (the default)
* Negative only: dwtest(model, alternative = "less")

The test provides a DW statistic (usually denoted as d) and a p-value.
DW Statistic (d): Ranges from 0 to 4.

* d approx 2: Suggests no autocorrelation.
* 0 <= d < 2: Indicates positive autocorrelation.
* 2 < d <= 4: Indicates negative autocorrelation.

Note: A range of 1.5 to 2.5 is generally considered acceptable for most models.


```{r, echo=FALSE}
dwtest(FI.lm, alternative = "two.sided")

```

## Check for Heteroscedasticity

The Breusch-Pagan test checks if the variance of the errors in the model is constant (homoscedasticity).

* Null Hypothesis (H0): The residuals have constant variance (homoscedasticity).
* Alternative Hypothesis (HA): The residuals do not have constant variance (heteroscedasticity).

Interpretation:

* P-value < 0.05: Reject the null hypothesis. There is significant evidence of heteroskedasticity.
* P-value > 0.05: Fail to reject the null hypothesis. The assumption of homoscedasticity holds.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
bptest(FI.lm)

```

## Diagnostic Plots

```{r , echo=FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

autoplot(FI.lm, which = 5:6, ncol = 2, label.size = 3)

ggplot(lm.data, aes(x = .fitted, y = .std.resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -2, linetype = "dashed")
  

```
